Abstract
Background/Aim
Acne is a common dermatological manifestation of polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), a prevalent endocrinological disorder among women of reproductive age. A growing body of evidence highlights glucose metabolism disorders, including insulin resistance, in the context of PCOS. This study aimed to investigate the association of acne and its severity with insulin resistance in a population of women with PCOS.
Patients and Methods
A total of 305 women with PCOS aged between 17-35 years were included in this retrospective observational study. Anthropometric, hormonal, biochemical, and ultrasonographic markers of PCOS were analyzed in relation to insulin resistance indices, including HOMA-IR and QUICKI.
Results
Acne was present in 56.4% of participants, with 52.1% exhibiting mild and 4.3% severe cases. Younger age (
p
=0.006), higher DHEAS levels (
p
=0.001), and glucose metabolism disorders, including fasting glucose >100 mg/dl,
p
=0.026 and 2-h glucose higher than 140 mg/dl (
p
=0.019), were significantly associated with acne. Multivariate analysis indicated younger age (OR=0.94,
p
=0.012), elevated DHEAS levels (OR=1.03;
p
=0.006), and 2-h glucose levels >140 mg/dl (OR=3.25,
p
=0.029) as independent predictors of acne severity.
Conclusion
This study indicates the association between insulin resistance and hyperandrogonemia with both the presence and severity of acne in PCOS. These findings align with contemporary literature and underscore the importance of addressing the hormonal and metabolic factors in the etiological management of acne in PCOS.
Keywords:
PCOS, acne, hyperandrogenism, insulin resistance, metabolism, metformin
Introduction
Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) is a prevalent endocrine disorder affecting women of reproductive age. It is estimated that approximately 8-13% of women in this demographic suffer from PCOS (
1
). Its principal manifestations include irregular ovulation and menstruation and subsequent female fertility limitations (
2
). PCOS manifestations may also affect the skin and its appendages resulting in excessive hair growth (hirsutism), thinning hair or hair loss as well as acne (
3
).
The prevalence of acne among women with PCOS ranges depending on the diagnostic criteria used to establish the diagnosis of the syndrome. Acne has been reported among 36 to 76% of women with PCOS as per the Rotterdam and National Institutes of Health (NIH) criteria, respectively (
3
,
4
). A meta-analysis of 60 studies, based on data from 240,213 patients, indicated an overall acne prevalence of 43% among this demographic (
3
). Acne in the context of PCOS can lead to long-term skin lesions with a lasting impact on patients’ appearance. Evidence suggests that this can significantly impact the quality of life and psychological well-being of affected women (
5
).
Pathophysiological pathways connecting PCOS and acne have been sought in the context of hyper-androgonism (
6
). The latter has been considered as a factor promoting increased and altered sebum production and follicular hyperkeratinization enabling microbial contamination of the sebaceous glands and contributing to acne-inducing chronic inflammation (
7
,
8
). Metabolic disorders associated with PCOS are also likely to contribute to acne development. In particular, insulin resistance and subsequent hyperinsulinemia seem to stimulate androgen production triggering the above-mentioned cascade. Simultaneously, increased glucose concentration has been found to be proportional to the severity of acne in women with PCOS (
9
,
10
).
Glucose-regulating agents including metformin, acarbose, and myoinositol have been shown to be effective against acne in the context of PCOS (
11
,
12
). Comprehending the impact of glucose metabolism disorders on acne development among patients with PCOS has a major potential to improve not only the understanding of the disease, but also the targeted management of acne through interventions focusing on metabolic health. It can also reduce the use of symptomatic acne treatment and their subsequent risk and cost for patients and healthcare systems.
This study investigated the association of glucose metabolism disorders and acne in women with PCOS followed up in a tertiary reference center in Greece.
Patients and Methods
Patients and measurements
. This is a retrospective observational clinical study based on a registry of young adults (17-35 years of age) with PCOS that attended the Gynecological Endocrinology - Child and Adolescent Gynecology outpatient clinic of a tertiary university hospital between January 2007 and December 2015. Patients were included in the study following baseline assessment that rendered them eligible for a PCOS diagnosis as per the Rotterdam ESHRE/ASRM-sponsored PCOS criteria.
The assessment included anthropometric and phenotypic characteristics as well as imaging (ultrasound) and laboratory findings. Weight and height were measured in kg and cm, respectively, with patients dressed lightly and standing barefoot on the same scale. For height measurements, subjects were positioned in the Frankfurt plane. A soft tape was used to measure waist circumference around the 12
th
rib and hip circumference around the iliac crest. Subsequently, the body mass index (BMI, kg/m
2
) and waist to hip ratio were calculated. Subjects were classified as normal-weight, overweight, and obese in accordance with the criteria set by the WHO. A BMI between 18.50 and 24.99 was defined as physiological weight, while a BMI of 25 to 29.99 was classified as overweight. Subjects with BMI values falling short of or exceeding these values were classified as underweight and obese accordingly. Phenotypic assessment included the degree of hirsutism as per Ferriman-Gallwey-Lorenzo (FGL) index (
13
). In this context, hair growth was evaluated in nine body parts leading to a score varying from a minimum of 0 to a maximum of 36, with scores higher than 6 being considered compatible with androgen excess.
Imaging assessment was conducted with transvaginal ultrasonography (US) performed between day 6-8 of the menstrual cycle. Ovarian morphology was assessed as per international standards to collect diagnostic evidence for PCOS (
14
).
Laboratory assessment of serum biochemical markers was performed at baseline with blood collection after overnight fasting approximately at 08.00 am. Testosterone, dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate (DHEAS) and cortisol levels were analyzed using Elecsys 1010/2020 and Modular analytics E 170 (Roche, Basel, Switzerland) with coefficients of variation (CV) of 5.6%, 6%, and 7%, respectively. Delta-4 Androstenedione (Δ4-A), 17-Hydroxyprogesterone (17-OHP), and free testosterone (FT) were analyzed with radioimmunoassay kits from Diagnostic Setters International Inc. (Webster, TX, USA), with a CV of 6.3%, 9.7%, and 9.75, respectively. Glucose levels were estimated using the colorimetric method for the quantitative measurement of glucose concentration in serum, plasma, and urine (Menarini diagnostics, Firenze, Italy), with a CV of 2.33%. Hormone measurements, including T4, T3, thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH), prolactin (PRL), follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH), and luteinizing hormone (LH) were analyzed using the ADVIA Centaur system with CVs of 3.44%, 5.55%, 5.87%, 4.8%, 3.9%, 2.7%, and 7.5%, respectively. Activated partial thromboplastin time (APTT) was measured using a clotting assay on the SIEMENS BCSC XP System Analyzer. These equipment and testing modalities were available at the laboratory facilities of the same tertiary center where the recruitment of the patients and their follow up were also performed. This protocol has been followed in previous studies by the authors’ department (reference - anonymized).
A number of indices were calculated for each patient following their assessment, in particular the HOMA insulin resistance (HOMA-IR), quantitative insulin sensitivity check index (QUICKI), Matsuda index of insulin sensitivity, and Lipid Accumulation Product (LAP). The following calculation formulas were applied:
• HOMA-IR Index=[(Fasting Insulin)×(Fasting Glucose)]/161, with insulin concentration expressed in pmol/l and glucose in mmol/l.
• QUICKI index=1/(log(fasting insulin)+log(fasting glucose)), with insulin concentration expressed in pmoles/l and glucose in mmoles/l.
• Matsuda index=10,000/(G0 X I0 X Gx X Ix)×0.5 with glucose and insulin values in mmol/l and pmol/l, respectively.
• LAP=(Waist circumference (cm)-58)×(Triglyceride concentration (mmol/l)).
Statistical analysis
. Quantitative variables were expressed as mean values (Standard Deviation) or as median (interquartile range), while categorical variables were expressed as absolute and relative frequencies. For the comparison of proportions, chi-square and Fisher’s exact tests were used. Student’s
t-
test or Mann-Whitney test was used for the comparison of continuous variables between two groups. Logistic regression analysis using a stepwise method (
p
for entry 0.05,
p
for removal 0.10) was used in order to identify factors associated with the presence of acne. Adjusted odds ratios (OR) with 95% confidence intervals (95%CI) were computed from the results of the logistic regression analyses. All reported
p
values are two-tailed. Statistical significance was set at
p
<0.05 and analyses were conducted using SPSS (IBM Corporation, Armonk, NY, USA) statistical software (version 27.0).
Ethics
. The study was planned and conducted in accordance with the 1964 Declaration of Helsinki and its later amendments and was approved by the Institutional Review Board (IRB: Anonymized).

Discussion
The present study aimed to investigate the relationship between glucose metabolism disorders and acne in women with PCOS. Because both acne and glucose metabolism disorders are common among women with PCOS, any potential interrelationship may offer improved treatment for both conditions. The study was a cohort analysis of young women with PCOS, evaluating various hormonal, biochemical, and clinical features to investigate their association with acne severity.
In this study, we identified a significant association between acne and PCOS, with hormonal and metabolic factors playing a very important role. Among women with PCOS, younger age, high levels of DHEAS, and insulin resistance markers such as fasting glucose >100 mg/dl and 2-h glucose >140 mg/dl, had a significant association with acne. Furthermore, the prevalence of acne was greater compared to the general population, in agreement with literature reports that identify acne as one of the most common dermatological manifestations of this syndrome.
These findings are in agreement with the large number of published papers indicating a high prevalence of acne among women with PCOS, ranging from 30% to 81% across various populations (
15
,
16
). Previous meta-analyses and reviews have also demonstrated a higher prevalence of acne in patients with PCOS compared to healthy women, with prevalence values as high as 43% among PCOS patients
versus
21% among controls (
3
,
7
).
The correlation between the severity of acne and increased androgen levels is well documented, which is consistent with our study, especially concerning the significant role of DHEAS in women with mild to severe grades of acne. Moreover, insulin resistance, another key feature of PCOS, was found to be related to acne. This further corroborates the findings of Franik
et al.
(
7
) and Shamim
et al.
(
16
), which suggest that metabolic disturbances exacerbate the disease.
However, not all studies agree on the specific hormonal markers associated with acne in PCOS. Some studies have been able to determine weaker correlations of acne with androstenedione, as well as other androgens (
16
